utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, you were going to be finishing with your cross-examination of the witness, Mr. Dzakula.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are reminded that you are pound by the pledge or the declaration that you made at the beginning of your evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, you testified about Operation Corridor; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that this operation took place in mid-1992. Would that be a fair assessment of what you said?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, roughly speaking, mid-1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us how was the corridor cut in half? Are you familiar with any details about this?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the road leading from Banja Luka to Serbia, that's at least what the media said was correct, had been cut off and could no longer be used to travel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Would it be right that in or around that time, UN forces arrived in UN-protected areas and the road had in fact been open until the moment it was cut off?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who blocked that road?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only share with you what I learned from the media. It was reported that this had been done by units belonging to the Croatian Defence Council, who were probably together with the Croats and the Bosniaks. That's what the media reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that sanctions had already been imposed by this time against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, composed of Serbia and Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What did these sanctions entail? Did they entail an end of all traffic and communication, air traffic, road traffic. In other words, the country itself being ostracised as it were?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What about this road through Bosnia that we mentioned? Was this not in fact the only road leading to the Republic of Serbian Krajina at the time and this road was used for all supplies, medicines, fuel, food, everything that the local population needed?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Since you were a member of the government of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, perhaps you're familiar with this. Did the government of the Republic of Serbian Krajina or indeed its president demand that the international community open that road so that the UN units could get all their supplies, all the supplies they needed?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Security Council established at the time that the units that had blocked that road were regular units of the Croatian army who had for some reason ended up in Bosnian territory?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that particular detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: If not in your capacity as a government member, then perhaps you might be familiar with this from the media, from the press, the public communications media. There was a dire shortage of nearly everything that prevailed, in the Banja Luka hospital 12 newborns died in their incubators because there was a shortage of oxygen and it wasn't possible to get it over from Belgrade and in the Knin hospital kidney patients died because no equipment was available to perform a dialysis.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read about this in the papers and in the media, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, do you know that when the so-called corridor was split in half, cut in half, the Serbian population suffered a great deal on the hands of the armed forces who had blocked the road?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard and seen media reports of this, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps remember this? The unit that Mr. Martic in his capacity as Minister of the Interior was with -- was this perhaps discussed at a session of the government? Did Mr. Martic perhaps ask approval to start an operation like this because there was no other way?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that but I was elsewhere in Western Slavonia and was not physically present at this particular meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Let's be specific about this, please. You heard this issue was indeed raised at this government meeting, as I phrased it myself?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dzakula. Do you perhaps know that there was an operation to re-establish traffic along that road and that during that operation many soldiers from the Republic of Serbian Krajina were killed and wounded?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even a single life seems like a huge waste, even when a single life is lost. Even that I would consider to be a huge waste. I don't know how many actually were killed but I do believe that a number of them were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it because of this particular result that he obtained that Mr. Martic later on enjoyed a great deal of respect and authority among the local population as someone who had waged a brave war with his soldiers and was eventually successful?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said. He enjoyed a great deal of authority and respect and he was promoted to the rank of General by Goran Hadzic, the president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and everything you asked me now about the corridor, what I know is based on media reports but there is something else I have to say. Once the corridor was blocked, the whole of the Posavina area was devastated, many houses were torched and many civilians were killed. Croat civilians too. There can't have been a good enough reason to torch all these villages, all these houses and devastate and destroy all these villages as part of the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you yourself take part in this fighting along the corridor?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wasn't personally involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What do you know about the intensity of fighting that went on along the corridor, about the number of units involved, which Croatian brigades, which BH army Brigades and which units on the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about media reports but I've never seen or heard anything that would constitute reliable information on what you're asking me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say you weren't physically present and were not aware of the intensity of the fighting. You knew nothing about the exact ratio of the warring parties. You know nothing about the circumstances under which the fighting occurred. How can you then say, sir, that there can't have been any reason for all this destruction? Destruction does not necessarily only come about as a deliberate act of damaging property.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not always deliberate. Sometimes it's a side effect of fighting. One thing that I would like to add is, I was in prison, I was there with some people who were involved in the fighting around the corridor and I heard accounts from them on how civilians had been killed. They didn't talk about thousands of civilians being killed but yes they did say that civilians had been killed. They were feeling greatly distressed about all those young men aged 20 or 21 being killed and they saw all those people who were steeped in crime around them. They said it was a huge shame. I know that every time there is a war, every time there is a battle, houses get torched and destroyed and so do villages. But what I'm saying sir, is that in this particular operation there was damage inflicted and destruction wrought in places where there was no direct fighting or combat. And this was the case in Posavina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: But isn't it the case that in every war there is vengeance and there is pointless crime, Mr. Dzakula? What do you have to say about that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That certainly is the case but there is always the obligation to pursue -- to try these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You held a high office in the prison [as interpreted], you had all the information. Did you ever report these people to anyone so that they could be tried?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please speak one at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. First of all the interpreters have just intervened, as the Court is well aware. But I think partly as a result of the speed and the overlap, I think the last question, there appears to be an error, at least in the translation that we've gotten, and maybe it could be rephrased.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The last question? Is that the question that says "you held a high office in a prison"?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Right. I assume that that's an error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It should be a high office in something else other than prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I would think so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do you think, Mr. Milovancevic? Was he a prison warder?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Obviously, Your Honour. Obviously there must be a mistake which is not deliberate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: High office in what? Can you tell us what high office did you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can re-ask the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, please ask the question again and once again, Mr. Milovancevic, slow down. Mr. Dzakula, wait for Mr. Milovancevic to ask his question and answer after he has stopped, and Mr. Milovancevic, wait for Mr. Dzakula to give his answer before you ask the next question. Thank you very much. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, I asked you if, as a highly -- high-ranking official, you did anything about these people who talked about their own crimes. It's a horrible thing. It's a huge responsibility on their shoulders?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object that -- the question misstates the evidence. Because we are talking clearly about the time period of the fall of 1993 and the witness has testified that he did not hold a high-ranking office at that time in the RSK government. He did have a position but I think counsel has misstated the evidence and I would also suggest that he's getting a little argumentative with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is being argumentative, Mr. Whiting, to say that it's a horrible thing, it's a huge responsibility on their shoulders?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I won't press that part of the objection, Your Honour, because now that I look at it, it just seemed to me heading in that direction. But I won't press that part. My objection that I will press is that the question misstates the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, the question misstates the evidence. What is your response?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in order to avoid having a discussion about all of this, the gist of my question was, Mr. Dzakula, as a responsible and educated person, having heard about these war crimes that had been committed from their direct perpetrators, knowing about the place and time of these crimes, did he inform anyone about this? Irrespective of his position, this would be a duty for any human being in that sort of situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's a completely different question, and I see Mr. Whiting is not objecting to that one. If Mr. Dzakula heard the question, will he please answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I held no office whatsoever at the time. I was in prison, I was being tried for treason and espionage. I lived like a hunted animal after that, as I said in my testimony. I had no opportunity whatsoever to share anything with anyone because anything I did was risky, constituted a life risk for me, any action that I might have taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, Operation Corridor took place in June 1992 and you were in prison in 1993, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Please allow me to complete my question. Does that mean that it wasn't until one year later that --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, there was a question and the witness tried to answer the question and then he was cut off by counsel, who apparently wanted to ask a different question. Maybe if counsel could allow the witness to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. I do think, Mr. Milovancevic, you can't cut the witness off. You asked a very complete question: "Mr. Dzakula, Operation Corridor took place in June 1992 and you were in prison in 1993, weren't you?" And you didn't allow the witness to -- can you answer the question, please? Will you please answer the question whether you were in prison at the time Operation Corridor took place in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Am I supposed to answer? Well, as I said a moment ago, I heard about this when I was already in prison, not in 1992. I knew nothing in 1992 about the specific crimes. I learned about this when I was in prison which was in late 1993. I had no opportunity to share anything with anyone. The only thing I could have risked in prison was losing my life. I was in the same section with people who killed one, two, three, four, five or more people. It would have made no sense for me to turn any of them in at the time. It would have constituted a great risk to myself and what those people saw in me was a person accused of treason, of high treason.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Didn't you tell us a while ago, Mr. Dzakula, that those murder he is, multiple murderers in some cases who there were in prison?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But those people were there because they had killed Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Would I be right, Mr. Dzakula, if I said that all of the appeals sent by the government of the Republic of Serbian Krajina to the international community, UNPROFOR, UNHCR, assistants of the Secretary General of the UN, the government of Yugoslavia, to have this road reopened, the road that was the life line of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, that all these appeals and attempts failed? Would I be right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, entirely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have nothing else to ask about this particular subject. Let's move forward a little, Mr. Dzakula. Let's go to 1995, January 1995. You mentioned in your testimony something called plan Z-4; is that right, Mr. Dzakula?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you say that this plan envisaged a high level of autonomy for Croatian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A high level of autonomy for the former SAO Krajina which means the best part of what then was the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this plan envisaged in relation to Western Slavonia? You were one of the high-ranking officers of the region before the war.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Immediate integration into the Republic of Croatia with no autonomy whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this plan Z-4 envisaged in relation to Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A five-year transitional period followed by integration into the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the former Serbian autonomous region of Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Srem, in addition to your own Western Slavonia were meant to be integrated back into the Republic of Croatia with no level of autonomy whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely what the whole thing meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What about the former SAO Krajina, the remains of the third part of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, the former SAO Krajina, the autonomy that was on offer, which part of the is SAO Krajina was that in relation to?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember all the municipalities. I'll try to list some. I'll start from the north. Dvor, [unintelligible], Glina, Dvornic [phoen], Vrgin Most, Plaski, Korenica, Lapac, Gracac, Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac, I think that's about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you remember the exact figure. How many predominantly Serb municipalities made up what used to be the Republic of Serbian Krajina? What was their number?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember their exact number. This was after all a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the report of the government of the Serbian autonomous region of Eastern Slavonia from 1992, where it is stated that in the course of 1991, in the operations conducted by Croatian military formations in the territory of Daruvar, Podravska Slatina, Grubisno Polje, Pakrac, Okucani municipalities 4.118 Serb houses were destroyed as well as 27 Serbian churches?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that, except it was not the government of Western Slavonia. Rather, the regional council.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the same document, Mr. Dzakula, do you remember that in that report dating from April 1992, it was also stated that in the territory of the entire former Yugoslav Republic of Croatia, over 80 Serbian Orthodox Churches had been destroyed in 1991?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You, as a long-time advocate for establishing the truth, for helping the victims, you as a high official of the Serbian democratic council, are you familiar with the report of the UN Secretary-General, Boutros Boutros-Ghali, from May 1993, stating that in Croatia, outside of the territory of SAO Krajina, 251.000 Serbs had been expelled only from urban areas or from urban areas alone?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did we conclude jointly yesterday that in the flash operation, in May of 1995, and in the storm operation in August of 1995, by means of brutal military operations conducted by Croatian forces, almost all Serbian inhabitants had been deported?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that yesterday, from the territory of Western Slavonia and the former SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Given these circumstances, do you still believe that the plan Z-4, which was on offer, was something that could be termed as acceptable for Serb population?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dzakula.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: No, that's all right. I understood you. Thank you. Are you familiar with the provision of Vance Plan from 1991 on the basis of which the UN peace forces were sent to the territory of the former Yugoslavia and deployed to the areas where there was a majority of the Serb population? Are you familiar with the provision specifying that the status of Serb territories would be resolved via negotiations without predetermining the outcome?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And finally, my last question, Mr. Dzakula: Are you familiar with the speech of the then-president of the Republic of Croatia, Mr. Franjo Tudjman, given at the main square in Zagreb, Jelacica square, on the first anniversary of inception of the new Croatian state in May of 1992, when he said that there would have been no war had Croatia not desired one, that Croatia estimated that it could only achieve its independence by means of war?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Dzakula. I have no further questions. Your Honours I have concluded my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Any re-examination, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to divide my questions into two groups. The first group of questions will be about events -- about things that you've talked about and events that occurred before August of 1991. The second group of questions will be about events that you talked about that occurred after August 1991. So let's start with the events that occurred before August 1991. You were asked on cross-examination a series of questions about non-Serbs who held positions in the military, in the government in 1990, and you answered a question about a Konrad Kolsek, and you agreed that he had been the 5th military district commander in 1990. Do you know what happened to him in 1991?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was replaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How about Aleksandar Spirkovski, a Macedonian who you agreed with Defence counsel that he was the Belgrade district military commander in 1990. Do you know how long he kept his position?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was also replaced. I don't know how long he stayed in office.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You also spoke about Anton Tus, who you said or agreed was the commander of the air force in 1990. Do you know when he left his position?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: By August of 1991, Mr. Dzakula, do you know the ethnicity of the military district and operational group commanders in the JNA at that time? By August of 1991.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were Serbs, as far as I remember. They were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You were also asked some questions about some political leaders. For example, you were asked about Stjepan Mesic. Now, do you know when he actually became the president of the Presidency of the SFRY? Do you remember what year that was?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You testified on cross-examination that his nomination was challenged, but there wasn't any follow-up question to that. Can you tell us who challenged his nomination?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The issue of his nomination or appointment were challenged by Borislav Jovic who was the Serbian member of the Presidency and Slobodan Milosevic who was then president of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Before Mr. Mesic actually became president of the Presidency of the SFRY, do you know if the Serbian bloc, that is Serbia and Montenegro, did anything with respect to the SFRY Presidency?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that there was a change, there were personnel changes among the members of the Presidency but I don't remember the details. I remember, however, that some changes were made in order to ensure that there would be four representatives. Some changes were implemented relating to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did -- do you remember if the Serbian bloc remained within the SFRY Presidency?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a while they would go out, storm out, and then come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you ever hear the term "rump Presidency"?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. That's what it was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What did that refer to, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, this term was used for the four representatives in question, those from Serbia, Montenegro, Kosovo, and Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what did they do -- what did they do that resulted in the rump Presidency or that related to the rump Presidency or what's the relationship? Can you explain further what ...

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that they made some personnel changes. They wanted to replace the member of the Presidency from Kosovo and Vojvodina, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not Mr. Mesic had any real power within the SFRY Presidency when he finally did assume the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I heard from the media, he had none.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You testified about a statement that you agreed you had heard was made by Mr. Mesic in October of 1991 to the effect that he had accomplished his task and Yugoslavia ceased to exist. Do you know if in the spring of 1991, at the time of this rump Presidency, Milosevic said anything about Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You were also asked about Ante Markovic who you agreed was the Prime Minister of the SFRY for a time, including in 1990. Do you recall hearing about a programme which he described as a reform programme that he proposed at the end of 1989?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of us followed his programme very attentively. We were hoping that it was a good programme for Yugoslavia and all of its citizens. I remember that for the first time, dinar became a hard currency, convertible currency.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know what Slobodan Milosevic's position was with respect to that reform programme?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't support it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: By 1991, do you know what kind of power, if any, Ante Markovic had within the government of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic? You may --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Every Prime Minister has authority stemming from the constitution. So there are authorities which stem from the constitution and then there are also factual ones or de facto authorities. Therefore I would like my learned friend to be more specific and to indicate precisely which ones he had in mind. Otherwise, the question is vague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any response, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, think it's been established that he did in fact hold the position so the question obviously is, did he have any real power within that position. I think the question was specific. I think the witness has answered it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did the witness answer? What did he say?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: He said he didn't. He answered before the objection was articulated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know when Mr. Markovic left the government?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to be as specific as possible. I believe it was in early 1992. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you were also asked on cross-examination about a number of questions about steps that were taken by the Croatian government before August 1991 relating to the coat of arms, the constitution, the flag, and steps that were taken towards independence. Do you remember those questions and your answers to those questions?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. If necessary, perhaps that can be repeated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I just meant generally, just to orient you to the topic. You also testified that after some of these steps had already been taken, you took the initiative in June and July of 1991 of creating the Serbian Democratic Forum with the goal of seeking a peaceful solution to the conflict. Could you explain to the Court why you thought that was possible in June and July of 1991?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believed that that was possible, not only because Serbs did not live only in the territory of Slavonia, Banija, Kordun, and I believed that if we started negotiations and dialogue and if we pointed out all of these - unfavourable to the Serbs - actions that were conducted, that we would gain the support of the intellectuals and some other people because at the time it was the policies of Milan Babic and Franjo Tudjman that dominated and those positions were extreme ones. We wanted to recruit other forces and to do other things in order to prevent the war, which was approaching. We believed firmly in this and we thought that it was our obligation as intellectuals, as citizens, those who belonged to the SDS and Jovan Raskovic, we thought it was our duty to make that attempt because we knew that both Serbs and Croats were afraid and we knew that both Serb and Croat citizens of Croatia were held hostage to those two types of policies which were almost identical, although opposed to each other. We had to do it because, gentlemen, in 1941 I have to give you an example of what happened then. Ante Pavlic slit throats of Serbs, torched villages, and Serbs, together with Croatians, joined the Partisan movement and fought for freedom. After all these tragedies, after killing and burning they found enough strength to fight jointly for common freedom. And therefore, we believed that before the conflict actually erupted, in order to prevent it, that we should go and try to find brave, smart people and there were such among Croats, who could help us avoid the domination of these two extreme political forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, once again, can I ask you to slow down. You made a long -- gave a very long answer there, and I can understand that it became emotional and your voice was raised, but also your speed increased. If you can just please reduce your speed. I don't mind your emotions going up but just slow down your pace.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, you were also asked a number of questions about the reaction that Serbs had to the steps that were being taken by the Croatian government in 1990 concerning the flag and the constitution and steps towards independence, and you testified that the Serbs you said were stunned and not pleased. I want to ask you about how the Serbs felt about the extremist leaders, as you have described them, on the Serb side and let's start in 1990 with the area of Western Slavonia. Did the Serbs -- in your estimation, did the Serbs in Western Slavonia support the extremist leaders on the Serb side in 1990?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't support them. Those of us who were involved in politics in Western Slavonia at the time, and also the Serbian population of Western Slavonia, and also Banija and Kordun, all of us were certainly afraid, we were intimidated by the Serb extremists displaying their Chetnik symbols. It was alien to us and it was as alien to us as the Ustasha symbols. We didn't want anybody to identify us with that. However, we were aware of the fact that the Croatian then political elite couldn't -- didn't want to miss the opportunity to generalise things and to portray all Serbs in that manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, you testified on cross-examination that around June of 1991, when Slovenia declared its independence, that the JNA under the direction of the SFRY leaders withdrew from Slovenia. My question is: Was there a significant Serb population living in Slovenia at that time?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were. There were a lot. There was a significant number. Slovenia was economically quite a developed country and a lot of Serbs and others went to work there, those from Bosnia, Croatia, and other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What was the majority population in Slovenia, in terms of ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slovenians.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, okay. Now we are up to -- now I'd like to ask you questions -- those are the questions about events that occurred before August of 1991. Now I'm going to turn to questions about events that occurred after August of 1991. You were asked some questions about JNA soldiers who were killed at the Korana bridge in Karlovac. Can you tell us how you heard about this?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard it from the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And with the assistance of the usher we could put it on the ELMO. The ERN of this map is 05013937 and in addition, I also have -- would ask the usher provide copies to the Bench. Defence counsel has already been provided with copies of this map. It's map 3 in the map book that we provided to Defence counsel. It's upside down on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Just to orient the Court and the parties and I'm not going to ask you to mark this. Just for the benefit so we can see where you're talking about, can you just point out for us where Karlovac is? First of all let me ask you, Mr. Dzakula, do you recognise this map?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. Republic of Croatia and Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And is this how the Republic of Croatia looked in terms of the municipality divisions in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Could you just show us where Karlovac is on the map, just so we are oriented.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates] Right here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you testified on cross-examination that the perpetrators in this case had been charged and are currently on trial. Who are the alleged perpetrators in the case?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the reserve forces or the police of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where are they on trial, if you know?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You were also asked about a family by the name of Zec or Zec, I'm not sure about the pronunciation, that was killed by -- that you said was killed by Croatian extremists in Zagreb in October of 1991. Can you tell us how you heard about that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was written about in the Republic of Croatia, quite extensively. The media condemned that and it was quite well publicised.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Which media condemned that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croatian media as well, Feral Tribune was the most vociferous one and there were others who wrote about it as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said on cross-examination that the perpetrators were investigated and tried. Do you know anything about the alleged perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the Zec family?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I heard from the media was that they were members of the security detail of Franjo Tudjman. As a result of that, when they were questioned -- perhaps I won't explain it in proper legal terms but the story was that some legal errors were made in investigation or during the questioning. Allegedly their attorneys were not present when they were questioned. At any rate, this led to their acquittal, these procedural errors, and due to that, a deal was struck with the Zec family. They received some kind of a compensation. This is what I learned from the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And just to be clear, were the alleged perpetrators Croats or Serbs?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I have probably about ten minutes more, maybe 15 at the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have 15. You have 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Should I -- I have tone or 15 minutes to go. Should I continue? I see we are -- oh, no I'm sorry, I actually should be able to finish then. I misread the time. Could the witness please be shown Prosecution Exhibit 3, please? It's a map and I think it's not on the E-Court system. This is the map which we subsequently provided the translation for.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, could you just take a look at that map, please? Do you know who produced this map, who made this map?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says the army. It's written down here. Probably someone from the Republic of Serbian Krajina authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. That was my own question about that exhibit. You also -- you testified, Mr. Dzakula, you were asked questions about a number of Croat military operations that took place in 1992 and 1993 at Miljevac plateau, the Maslenica bridge and the Medak pocket and I'm just going to ask you a few questions about those operations and your testimony but before I do I just want to see if we can establish a little bit of terminology to make it easier. You've also testified about that the United Nations took control of certain areas within Croatia in the beginning of 1992. Can you tell us what those areas were called?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once the UN forces had arrived, they divided the Republic of Serbian Krajina into four sectors, sector west, Western Slavonia; sector east, Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, Western Srem; sector north, Banija and Kordun; and sector south, Lika and Dalmatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of the term pink zones?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell us please what the pink zones were?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on what I remember, these were zones or areas where the Serbs were not the predominant ethnic group. Rather, Croats had succeeded by military operations to -- in constituting a majority in these areas. And that is why the UN had to deploy their own units in the shape of ink spots.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know if the pink zones were within the UN-protected areas or were they outside of the UN-protected areas?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are talking about ink spots here, so they were considered protected zones as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand the ink spots were considered protected zones. But what about the pink zones? Do you know if they were considered protected zones?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you testified about the operation at Miljevac plateau in June of 1992. And if we could -- well, first let me ask you this: Can you tell us if you know where in Croatia this is? In terms of municipality or sector.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is sector west. I think it's around Sibenik or Zadar, that general area, but I can't be more specific. Rather, this is sector south. I'm sorry. Zadar, Sibenik. I don't know the area. It's along the border somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell us how you heard about the events there in June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard media reports also, when I came to a government meeting, the families of some of the missing started coming. There was a government meeting where appeals were made to find these people, their sons, whatever. They spoke about this operation, they said this was quite a surprise. The people who were in position there were killed, and for a long time, nobody knew their whereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You also testified about the Maslenica bridge operation in January of 1993. Can you tell us where that is?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a bridge. It was under Serb control. It's down somewhere near Obrovac, if I remember correctly, near the confrontation line between the Croats and the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How did you hear about what happened there?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First there were some media reports, and then when operation Maslenica occurred I was in Knin myself. We spent the night there because there was a government meeting the next day and we heard that Maslenica had been attacked. For this reason, the government meeting that was scheduled was never held. They told us that the positions had shifted and that Maslenica had been taken by the Croatian army. That was all I heard at the time. We parted ways. It wasn't possible to have a government meeting on account of all these newly arisen circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You were also asked questions about the Medak pocket operation in September of 1993. Can you tell us how it is you heard about that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I was in prison by this time. I heard about media reports seen or heard by people who were there with me in prison, I mean. I heard about the Medak pocket operation. I heard that some of the population there were killed and that houses were torched. There was a lot being written about that in Croatia. There was a trial and I think somebody was sentenced. I think it was General Norac, who was convicted, or, rather, the trial is about to take place. General Norac and General Ademi are about to be tried in Croatia about the Medak pocket. That's what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And those generals, Norac and Ademi, are they Croatian generals or Serb generals?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are Croatian generals.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You were asked some questions today about the Posavina corridor operation in 1992 in Bosnia-Herzegovina and you testified that you heard from later -- when you were imprisoned in the fall of 1993, that you heard from people who had participated in that operation or who had been witnesses. Could you elaborate a little bit more what it is you heard from those people?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no talk of any great deal of combat or of fighting. What I did hear was from a young man who was there for a day, and was then taken somewhere else. He started talking about how they were involved in the fighting around the corridor and that they came across many civilians, old hags, as he said, and were killing them. It was a brief statement that he made with no additional comments. Later on, however, when I travelled there myself, the Posavina corridor, I realised that it had been razed to the ground, devastated, and laid waste. This is a long and wide area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, you also testified that at this time, there were sanctions against Serbia-Montenegro. Do you know why there were sanctions, UN sanctions?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the sanctions were imposed because of the use of the air force and the shelling of Sarajevo, the war in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know if medicines were covered by the sanctions or exempted by the sanctions?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, not. I think not. But I can't be certain. Something was always exempted that was a necessity. I know that even during sanctions, fuel would be allowed to come in for the harvest, something apparently so harmless.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In one of your responses to Defence counsel's questions you started to -- you offered to explain why you thought the Z-4 plan was still possible or still acceptable under the circumstances -- given its terms. And -- but you were not invited to give that explanation. Could you tell us now what -- why you thought it was acceptable or workable or what it was you wanted to explain?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, above all, what I had in mind was that, when this plan Z-4 was first tabled by the people who had produced it and when the plan was turned down, even for consideration, that was a mistake. I believe the plan was worth considering and publishing in the Serbian Krajina, and people should have been given a chance to give their opinion on the plan. More time should have been allotted to analyse the plan, to speak about what the real possibilities were and which of all the options on offer were really feasible and what the ambitions were. If you had a plan like that, the one that was tabled, and this plan was never even considered, I think this was extremely irresponsible. I know that we Serbs were diffident about the Tudjman government but that situation was not sustainable. It would have been impossible for Western Slavonia to cut Croatia in half and to have its own country in the area. This should have been cut down to size, to fit a more realistic framework. Ambition is one thing, reality is an altogether different thing. Attempts should have been made to reach some sort of common ground. What we are witnessing nowadays and we should have known this even back then, at the time, Croatia, Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, all these former Yugoslav republics, with the exception of Slovenia which is now part of Europe, they are on their knees begging to be allowed in as soon as possible, all these governments. All the borders that we wanted to pull up would have become meaningless. It would have been important for all those people to stay where they were for a peaceful resolution to the conflict, to have all the refugees back, for life to go back to normal. I think this plan known as plan Z-4, if this had been accepted and we see that it was later accepted because it was later accepted, I'm sorry that it's late now, and I'm sure that it doesn't justify the operations that took place later on. I'm not trying to justify them, but it's a huge mistake. It's a huge mistake by the Krajina leadership to have turned down that plan and not to even have considered it. I didn't approve that in Western Slavonia. My people didn't approve of that move. They wanted at least to be given an opportunity to see what the plan was offering so that they could speak their own minds.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Dzakula, I just have just two or three questions on one last topic and I hope you'll forgive me that it's a little bit of a personal topic. You testified on cross-examination about your family, what happened to your family in World War II, and you testified that your parents were in a camp in World War II. Could you tell us which camp they were in?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the massacre in the village of Dreza, where my father hails from, and Kusonje, my mother's village, members of their families had been killed and thrown into wells and the remaining members ended up in a camp in Stara Gradiska. These were camps in the Jasenovac district. My father ended up in Sisak. Three of his own brother were killed there and some other members of his family, without going into that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could the witness just please slow down a little because I'm not -- I'm no longer keeping track of all these names and locations and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My parents, when they were still children, together with their own grandparents were taken away to camps, to a camp in Stara Gradiska and a camp in Sisak, alongside with many other children from those villages who were being taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How did your parents survive the camp?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My father was saved by a Croat who hailed from Crkveni Bok near Sisak. He took him home to his own house and he fed him until the end of the war. My mother was saved by Josip Delic from Filipovac, Pakrac municipality. She later left for a different Croatian family, Krusevar, and stayed there until the end of the war. My parents had been taken to camps by the Ustasha. Their entire families had been wiped out by the Ustasha. 17 of my father's family were killed. It was only he and his sister who remained alive, who survived, and yet they were saved by Croats who rescued them from the camps. My parents taught me --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That was going to be my question. What did your parents teach you?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My parents taught me that what the Ustasha did to them was one thing. The other thing was the Croats who helped them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula. Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and I apologise for going over the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. Whiting. We will take a break. We will come back at five past four. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, could the witness be excused?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Actually, before we excuse the witness and before we retire for a short break, what do you intend doing with this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I neglected to act on that map. If it could be moved into evidence, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. The map may be then admitted into evidence and be given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. That would be Exhibit number 19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Court adjourned. Come back at five past four.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry again, but did you want the witness back or did you want him excused?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We do want him back.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, you'll have a few questions from the Chamber. Judge Hoepfel will ask questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Dzakula, please. In your chief examination, you mentioned on Monday, 16th, at several times in connection with the title of the accused, Mr. Martic, the ministry -- a ministry, you called the Ministry of Police and the Minister of Police. So as in page 363 on the transcript of 16th of January, 363 to 364, when you spoke about your arrest, the arrest on the 21st of September 2003, you said "in the morning hours, I was arrested by the assistant Minister of Serb Krajina, Krsta Zarkovic, who brought a group of members of a special unit in Knin. They arrested me and took me to Knin." And on the question of Mr. Whiting, that you described Krsta Zarkovic as an assistant minister. Assistant Minister of what? You said assistant Minister of Police, assistant to the then-minister, Milan Martic. Could you then please clarify what you meant under Minister of Police? Is this a Minister of the Interior or Minister of Defence or a special sort of minister? You then mentioned it at several other occasions, speaking of the Minister of Police. On pages 366 to 68, and then 370 to 71 and 399 to 400, Minister of Police or Ministry of Police. If you would clarify what you meant by that term, I would appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, we say Minister of Police but what that actually means is Ministry of the Interior. It's like an abbreviation. That's what people say. It's a term that people use so they call them Ministry of Police. It's that simple.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So second -- this meaning also, your statement of 17th of January, at page 424, line 25 to 425, line 15, where you talked about how Mr. Martic behaved as a minister in the RSK government from February 1992 to February 1993. Which kind of minister did you mean in this connection? Is it the same category?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's the same ministry. It's the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let me ask you a third question, going back to the interrogation of 16th of January about this arrest on the 21st of September. Having mentioned -- having -- to have been brought to Knin to be arrested, to have been arrested and have been taken to Knin by a group of members of a special unit in Knin. Mr. Dzakula, do you know the name of that unit and to which organisation they belonged?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this unit was part of the Ministry of the Interior. The term "special police unit" was often used at the time. I'm not sure about its exact meaning but the term was widely used and this is also how these people referred to themselves. What was peculiar about them is their weapons. They didn't merely carry pistols. They had long-barrelled weapons too and armour piercing weapons. I'm not sure what these are called exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, there was a reference in your evidence yesterday to the TO and membership of the TO. I'd like to know what the TO is or what it refers to. Could you please explain to the Chamber for me?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, TO is an abbreviation that stands for Territorial Defence. Territorial Defence comprised two different kinds of units used for defending the country, the JNA on the one hand and the TO throughout the republics, municipalities, and local communes. This was a form of reserve force of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm most grateful to you, Mr. Dzakula.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, my questions might be a little funny because you might think that these are things that ought to be known but please bear with me. I'm trying to put everything in place in my mind. On the very first day and unfortunately I'm not able to get back to the line, you made reference to two parties, the one, the SDS, which you called the Serbian Democratic Party, and the other, the SDP, which you referred to as the party of democratic change. Did you belong to any one of these?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I belonged to the League of Communists of Croatia up until a few months before the war broke out. Later on, this party, Croatia's league of communists had its name changed into SDP which means party of democratic change. At the first multi-party elections, I voted for the SDB, for the party of democratic change which was the former League of Communists of Croatia. I was not a member at the time I voted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good, yeah, I remember you saying so. And the SDS? Who belonged to it? Or let me ask you a very specific question. Did Mr. Martic belong -- which party did Mr. Martic belong to, to your knowledge, if any?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: SDS is the Serbian Democratic Party. I don't know whether Mr. Martic was a member of that party and if so when he became. I don't know either whether he was a member of the League of Communists of Croatia. Most of the people employed in the police force at the time were but I cannot claim with certainty that Mr. Martic was as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The reason I'm asking you, today, let me say today, and I think it's at page 3 of today, line 22, I'm not able to get to it. I would read what you said -- read to you what you said but the question that was put to you in cross-examination at that line suggested that you and Mr. Martic were in the same government. You said, the question was, "Do you perhaps remember this? The unit that Mr. Martic in his capacity as Minister of the Interior was with, was this perhaps discussed at a session of the government? Did Mr. Martic perhaps ask approval to start an operation like this because there was no other way?", suggesting that you might have discussed it in the same government as Mr. Martic, you were sitting in the same government. Did you ever sit with Mr. Martic in the same government?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Martic and I were both members of the government of the Republic of Serbian Krajina starting from the 26th of February 1992, until late February 1993, at which time I was replaced. So we were members of the cabinet. He was the Minister of the Interior and I was vice-Prime Minister of the government, in charge of forestry and agriculture. I did not attend that particular session of the government, discussing the corridor, because at that time I was in Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Dzakula. Now, you also stated, Mr. Dzakula, in your evidence, that on the 2nd of October 1993, you were released from prison by order of the investigating judge but that on the same day, you were arrested again in Kostajnica and returned to the police station there. Do you know who it was who arrested you and to which organisation he or they belonged?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, at the border crossing between Republika Srpska and Republic of Serbian Krajina, I was arrested by the Serbian police with headquarters in Kostajnica. They were members of the Ministry of the Interior and they took me to the police station in Kostajnica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: They were members of the Ministry of Interior, is that what you say?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is this the same Ministry of Interior under Mr. Martic? Or was Mr. Martic the Minister of Interior at the time?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then you said also that when you were released on the 3rd of December 1993, you were again arrested and detained for several hours. Do you know who it was who arrested you on that occasion and to which organisation that person belonged?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 3rd of December 1993, I was released from prison, Your Honour. On the 4th of December, another arrest warrant was issued to arrest me and my colleagues. The arrest warrant was issued by the Ministry of the Interior. We received it from the police secretary for Western Slavonia region, Mr. Vaso Ostolucanin. At that time I was not arrested. I was in hiding for 50 days in order to avoid my arrest. Later on, on the 4th of February 1994, I was kidnapped in Belgrade. When I said "kidnapped," I do so because the persons wearing civilian clothes who approached me to take me into custody did not produce any IDs, did not say that they were any officials. They simply told me to go into -- with them into parked vehicles. I put up resistance and they used physical force and beat me and dragged me away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt you? That is the next question I'm going to ask. Can we finish the 3rd of December first before we go to the 4th of February the following year? You said now that the arrest warrant was issued by the Ministry of the Interior. Who was the Minister of the Interior at the time of the issue of that arrest warrant, the arrest warrant of the 3rd of December 1993?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Martic was Minister of the Interior at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's get to the 4th of February now.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 4th of February, Your Honour, in 1994, when I was kidnapped in Belgrade at 11.30, these persons who did so did not identify themselves. To this day, I don't know their identity. They wore civilian clothes. They turned me over to another three civilians on the same day, in the afternoon, and they said that they were from Western Slavonia. Now, as to whether they were members of some special police force or something else, I don't know. However, they took me to Knin, to the offices of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, and you also testified about Knin and that the next day, two men in camouflage uniforms came and took you to -- I think to a building in Knin. Do you know who these men were and what organisation they belonged to, the one in camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know their names. They said that they were members of the security, and by this, they meant the security services or secret service, which belongs to the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much, Mr. Dzakula. I don't have any further questions for you. Are there any questions arising from the questions by the Chamber from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: From the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you very much for coming, Mr. Dzakula. You are excused. You may stand down from the witness box.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness will be handled by Mr. Black but I'm wondering if before we call the next witness we could discuss the schedule for this witness. And I don't want to speak for the Defence but from conversations I've had with the Defence I understand that there is a concern about being prepared for this witness. I think there is a solution, though, because of the way the timing has worked out this week. What I would anticipate is that this witness would -- would give the bulk of his evidence today and tomorrow. He may even finish tomorrow, though I think there is -- it's more likely that he'll carry into next week just a little bit but in any event he will not finish before the end of the day tomorrow. And therefore, the Defence would not have to do the cross-examination of this witness until next week, Thursday at the earliest. I would hope that that break between today and tomorrow and Thursday would give the Defence enough time for the cross-examination but if we just -- and then that will effect the rest of our scheduling as to whether we bring witnesses and so forth. I just want to be sure we are all on the same page in terms of the schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you want the Court to ascertain with the Defence whether that arrangement would suit them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, please, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic works that suit you, if this witness gave his evidence-in-chief today and tomorrow and you would only begin your cross-examination sometime next week around Thursday, would be ready to cross-examine the witness by then?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in order for the Trial Chamber to understand the position of the Defence, I will highlight only two separate issues. One has to do with the expert report. Pursuant to the ruling of the Chamber of the 13th of January this year, this is introduced into evidence, including almost all of the transcripts from the Milosevic case except for some pages concerning which this witness will be heard live, and the Defence can cross-examine on this. In accordance with the pre-trial ruling of the Trial Chamber, the OTP has to provide the witness list prior to the 25th of December 2005. However, that wasn't done until the 2nd of January 2006. That's one problem. Another problem is that only a few days ago, the OTP informed us that this witness will be a fact witness. However, we did not receive the written statement of this witness as a fact witness, and this is in violation of Rule 66(A)(ii). This means that the beginning of testimony of this witness would be contrary to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence and prejudicial to the Accused. That's one issue. The second issue, Your Honour, is the state of readiness of Defence. I think that you know the majority of issues concerning this and we are very grateful to your intervention in that regard. What I also want to reiterate is this: When it comes to creating all the necessary material conditions for the work of the Defence, this is something that needs to be done at the very beginning of the trial. This trial began on the 12th of December 2005. The registry informed us on the 14th of December that we had to submit a formal invoice for them to pay an advance to us. I want to say, concerning this, that this invoice that we were supposed to send does not need any further review. We sent a letter to the Registry on the 5th of January and we asked them kindly, Your Honours, to bear in mind the fact that the trial is about to restart on the 16th of January. We were scheduled to arrive in The Hague on the 12th of January and we asked them to ensure that the funds were ready on the 12th of January. It is quite possible that the procedure in the registry is such that it is quite lengthy. However, the Registry never warned us about the fact that they were unable to provide funds for us in a timely fashion. Had we been informed on time we would have perhaps looked for some other possible solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I please -- I thought you were going to be very brief on that point and that's the point on which you're dwelling for a very long time. We have discussed that point. We discussed it yesterday, sir. And, please, let's not burden the record with things that we have discussed. We resolved this issue yesterday that you're going to be paid this week sometime. If you haven't been paid by today, I would expect that you would be paid tomorrow. And if that doesn't happen, then you have cause to complain once again. But I think we have dealt with that last point yesterday exhaustively. I would like to go back to the point -- first two points that you raised. Can we just remind the Chamber what ruling or what decision that you were referring to of the 13th of January that allowed evidence into the record which is just coming in like that, the way you explained? That was your first point. You said, in terms of a ruling of this Chamber, on the 13th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that was the Trial Chamber's decision on introducing the expert report dated 13th of January 2006, into evidence, as well as the transcript of this witness's testimony in another case. The reason I mentioned this is that I didn't really want to re-discuss the funds. All I wanted was to point out to you that the Defence finds itself in a very difficult situation where we are supposed to cross-examine a very sensitive expert witness, in view of the material that has to be covered, and the exhibits, a large number of exhibits that have to be introduced. The testimony of this witness is about to begin in the situation when the Defence is not ready for his testimony, in view of all of the circumstances that I have mentioned so far. If you would allow me to conclude, I wanted to add that our request is that this witness begin his testimony at a later date. He is, after all, an employee of the OTP, and he can come at any later date. Perhaps we will use a day and a half of work now, but this will save us time in the future. It will enable us to prepare better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. Now I understand what you're saying. Your short answer is, you are not able to start your cross-examination of this witness next week, Thursday. That's the short answer. That's the answer, Mr. Whiting. It does look like the Defence is not in a position because of the three reasons that they've given to cross-examine the witness next Thursday. Do you have any alternative suggestion in terms of scheduling?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, no. We can't just bring witnesses on the drop of a hat, as the Court is well aware. I would respond -- I don't -- I would submit that the Defence has had sufficient time to prepare for this witness. The expert report of this witness was provided to the Defence almost a year ago. The Defence responded, obviously looked at -- read the report and filed a response to the report at that time. All of the exhibits that are going to go in through this witness, and the Court will be happy to hear that it's going to be a smaller number than all of the exhibits referred to in the report, are cited for the most part I think almost entirely in the report. Other exhibits that may go in through this witness have been -- we have told the Defence about that. We did -- it is true we did inform the Defence on January 2nd that this witness would be the second witness testifying. We had already told them in December who the first witness would be. And so by my count, they have had three and a half weeks since they knew about this witness, but by the time they have to cross-examine this witness next week, they will have had three and a half weeks' notice that this witness -- that they would have to cross-examine the witness. In any court in this building, that's more, by a factor of two, probably, than enough time to -- than is ordinarily given and that should be fluff time to prepare, especially given a witness whose report was disclosed almost a year ago and dealt with then and responded to and discussed in filings. The point about him being a fact witness is a very minor point. He's going to talk very briefly about things that he saw in Zagreb when he was stationed there in 1995. There is no -- he has not done a witness statement on that issue. We disclosed in letter form what he would be talking about. It's very brief. And so there is no violation of Rule 66(A)(ii) because, since there is no statement to turn over, the rule is not violated. If we had a statement we would turn it over but instead what we've done is told him what it will about and that is standard practices that witnesses -- if there is new information that a witness is going to talk about, we disclose either by a memo or a letter to the Defence to alert them. And this was done sometime ago and they've had certainly plenty of time to respond to that and it is nothing new about the Zagreb -- about what happened in Zagreb. It's nothing materially different. It's completely consistent with our evidence and the theory of the case. So I would submit that the Defence should -- there is no good reason for them not to be ready to cross-examine the witness flex week. I think it would be very undesirable for a lot of reasons to have the witness start, to give his direct testimony, and then for there to be a large break between that and his cross-examination. And I can go through those reasons, if the Court wishes. But it puts a real constraint on his work here at the Tribunal and I think also it is undesirable to have an enormous -- for everyone's preparation purposes, and attention, it's very undesirable to have a big break particularly with this kind of a witness, between his direct examination and the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I -- the Chamber does not wish to go into the arena on to whether or not the Defence should be able to cross-examine because they were given documents last year already. They say they are not able to, and I think there can be any number of reasons. And I'm not trying to speak on their behalf and I'm saying that indeed they may very well have read those documents, they may very well have filed their response, but they have already told us yesterday that a lot of the documents are in storage. I don't know whether documents relative to this witness are in storage or not. I really don't know. And that may need -- that they may need to refresh their memory from those documents. The thrust of the Chamber here is to solve the problem, as I hear the Defence, if the witness gives his testimony in chief at a later stage and I would imagine that a later stage would be no later than next week Thursday, because I heard Mr. Milovancevic saying? We lose this afternoon and tomorrow, that might save us a lot of time later. So I would -- from that, I infer that later stage means Thursday. I am saying, if this witness testifies on Thursday, and you, Mr. Whiting, have indicated that he would probably finish his evidence by tomorrow if he started today, then there is no reason for him not to finish by the 27th, and the following week, 30th, 31st, without a long break, he would be cross-examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That would be acceptable to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That was the suggestion of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
